title: Finance reduced to mathematical formulas
subtitle: DCF, WACC, terminal value and the valuation multiples
openingQuestion: Where is it clearest that finance reduces to mathematical formulas?
openingOptions: DCF, WACC, terminal value and the valuation multiples
Only the accounting side genuinely uses formulas
explanation: Many finance problems are simply discounting cash flows, comparing multiples and modelling risk with explicit formulas. The hard part is not the formula but choosing sensible input assumptions - because the final answer is extremely sensitive to those assumptions.

realWorldExample.description: When analysing a company, most of the work is putting reasonable assumptions into familiar formulas and then testing how sensitive the answer is to them.

quiz.question: What principle does a DCF mainly rest on?
options: Comparing against peers in the same industry to set a value
Future money has to be discounted back to today
Taking book value and multiplying by an industry factor
Adding up the forecast profits of every projected year
quiz.explanation: A DCF reduces to the present value of future cash flows: money arriving later is worth less today, and the discount rate is what converts one into the other. Comparing against peers is the multiples approach, which answers a different question and depends on the market pricing those peers correctly. Book value multiplied by an industry factor ignores cash generation altogether, and simply summing forecast profits drops the time value of money, which is the entire point of the exercise.

quiz.question: If the DCF formula is mathematically exact, why can two analysts using the same DCF model on the same company still arrive at very different valuations?
options: Because their calculation software rounds numbers differently
Because each of them uses a different version of the DCF formula
Because the input assumptions differ, not because the formula is wrong
Because the published financial data is not the same for both
quiz.explanation: DCF is an exact piece of arithmetic, but its inputs - growth rate, WACC, terminal growth - are all subjective judgements about the future. This is why 'finance is mathematics' is only half true: the formula is mathematics, but choosing the assumptions is business judgement. Rounding differences are immaterial at this scale, the formula has one standard form, and both analysts are working from the same published statements.

quiz.question: Two analysts run the same DCF formula on the same company and land 40% apart. Where does that gap come from?
options: From how many decimal places were kept during the calculation
From the order in which the steps of the formula were carried out
From the currency used to present the final result
From the growth assumption and the discount rate
quiz.explanation: The discounting formula itself is exact arithmetic. The difference always lies in the business judgement behind the input numbers, which is exactly where 'finance is mathematics' stops being true. Decimal places, step ordering and presentation currency cannot move a result by anything close to 40% - they are the kind of explanation that sounds technical while leaving the real driver untouched.

quiz.question: Which skill matters more than fast calculation when working with financial models?
options: Asking the right questions about the basis and sensitivity of assumptions
Recalling the exact discounting formula for each valuation method
Moving quickly through a spreadsheet to cut model-building time
Memorising the average valuation multiple for every industry
quiz.explanation: The formulas already exist and a computer handles them instantly, so an analyst's real value lies in choosing and stress-testing the assumptions - the part the machine cannot do for you. Recalling formulas and moving fast through a spreadsheet are useful mechanics, and industry multiples are worth knowing, but none of them protects you from an assumption that was never questioned.

quiz.question: In a DCF model, which assumption usually has the largest effect on the final answer?
options: The revenue level forecast for the first year of the detailed projection period
The perpetual growth rate and the discount rate used in the terminal value
The tax rate applied to operating profit in each individual year
The number of years projected in detail before the terminal value is computed
quiz.explanation: Terminal value typically accounts for six to eight tenths of total value, and it sits inside a formula with the difference (WACC − g) in the denominator. A small shift in either of those two assumptions moves the answer a great deal - which is why that is the cell the sensitivity table has to focus on. The first-year revenue, the tax rate and the projection length all matter, but each affects only a slice of the value rather than the dominant block.

keyTakeaways: DCF and multiples are the two important frameworks
The input assumptions determine the valuation

summary.action: The input assumptions determine the valuation

sections.text: Many finance problems - from DCF to WACC - are at bottom explicit mathematical formulas. But the hardest thing in finance is not the arithmetic.
The formula is right; the assumptions are what decide the answer

DCF is an exact piece of mathematics - discounting future cash flows back to today. Yet two analysts running the same DCF model on the same company can still reach very different valuations, because the inputs (growth rate, discount rate, terminal value) are subjective judgements about the future rather than fixed numbers. This is why 'finance is mathematics' is only half true: the formula is mathematics, but choosing the assumptions is business judgement.

items: Many finance problems (DCF, WACC, multiples) rest on explicit mathematical formulas
The final answer is extremely sensitive to the input assumptions, not to the formula itself
The most important skill is not calculation but choosing sensible assumptions and testing their sensitivity

sections.title: Why one DCF formula produces two very different answers
sections.equation: Value = Σ (Cash flow in year t ÷ (1+r)^t)

example.title: Two analysts, one company
example.calculation: Analyst A: growth 8%, r = 10% · Analyst B: growth 4%, r = 12%
example.explanation: The discounting formula is identical on both sides. The difference lies entirely in two assumed numbers: the growth rate and the discount rate - judgements about the future, not calculations you can verify on the spot the way you can check a sum.

sections.text: Three kinds of finance problem, three levels of certainty

items: Pure calculation: compound interest, the future value of a known amount at a fixed rate - this really is just mathematics, and the answer is not up for debate.
Formulas with input assumptions: WACC, DCF, NPV - the formula is exact but the inputs are forecasts, so the result is subjective even though it looks precise to the last unit.
Qualitative judgements that resist quantification: management quality, durable competitive advantage - these shape the assumptions in the second layer but have no formula of their own.

sections.label: The skill actually worth practising
sections.text: Not calculating quickly and accurately - computers have done that better than people for a long time. The real skill is knowing how to interrogate an assumption: what is it based on, how sensitive is the final answer to it, and if it is wrong, which direction of error is the dangerous one.

lines: The formulas of finance are not the hard part.
Choosing the right input assumptions - and knowing how sensitive the answer is to them - is the real skill.

practicePrompt.question: The Discounted Cash Flow formula converts an asset into a value based on which core finance principle?
options: Asset value equals the PV of all its future cash flows
Asset value equals exactly what was paid for it in the past
Asset value is set by the seller and has nothing to do with cash flow
Asset value equals the share price multiplied by 10
practicePrompt.explanation: The core principle of DCF: 'a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow'. The value of an asset is the sum of its future cash flows discounted back to present value at the cost of capital, WACC. Historic cost describes what was paid, not what the asset is worth now, and a price set by the seller is an asking price rather than a valuation.
